{"needed": true, "prompt": "Scope: implement per-resource REST endpoints (GET, PUT/PATCH, DELETE, POST) server-side authorization and ownership semantics for a resource that contains owner_id. Do not change client code. Assume an authentication layer that provides current_user object with at least: id (owner id) and is_superuser (boolean). Implementation instructions:

1) Common principles and ordering
- Always authenticate first; ensure current_user is available in the request context.
- For every single-resource endpoint that takes resource_id: first attempt to fetch the resource by id from storage (ORM/DB). If no record found -> return HTTP 404.
- After confirming existence, apply ownership and permission checks as described below. Do checks in this order to avoid information leakage.
- For creation (POST): do not accept or trust any owner_id provided by the client. Server must set owner_id = current_user.id before storing.

2) Single-resource GET (read)
- Fetch resource by id; if not found -> 404.
- If resource.owner_id == current_user.id -> allow read (200 + resource payload).
- Else (resource owned by someone else):
  - If current_user.is_superuser == true -> allow read (200 + resource payload).
  - Else (normal user) -> return HTTP 404. Do not return 403, to avoid revealing the resource exists.

3) Single-resource PUT/PATCH (update)
- Fetch resource by id; if not found -> 404.
- If resource.owner_id == current_user.id -> allow update. Apply normal update validation and persist changes. Return 200/204 per your API style.
- Else (resource owned by someone else):
  - If current_user.is_superuser == true -> deny with HTTP 403 and response body exactly containing a JSON error detail with key detail and value "Read-only access" (e.g. {"detail":"Read-only access"}).
  - Else (normal user) -> return HTTP 404.
- Implementation note: ensure server disregards any client-supplied owner_id in the update payload. Prevent owner transfer via update unless there is a separate, explicit owner-transfer flow.

4) Single-resource DELETE
- Fetch resource by id; if not found -> 404.
- If resource.owner_id == current_user.id -> allow delete. Return 204 (or 200 per project convention).
- Else (resource owned by someone else):
  - If current_user.is_superuser == true -> deny with HTTP 403 and body {"detail":"Read-only access"}.
  - Else -> return HTTP 404.

5) Create (POST)
- Require authentication.
- Ignore client-supplied owner_id; set resource.owner_id = current_user.id (server-side) before insert.
- Persist and return 201 with created resource.

6) Error body and status conventions (explicit requirements)
- For superuser attempts to PUT/PATCH/DELETE others' resources: return HTTP 403 with JSON body exactly containing detail = "Read-only access" (e.g. {"detail": "Read-only access"}).
- For any access to non-existent resource: return HTTP 404.
- For normal user attempts to access another user’s resource (read/update/delete): return HTTP 404. Do not return 403 for normal users when accessing others’ resources.

7) Authorization helper / middleware recommendation (pseudocode)
- Implement a reusable helper function check_resource_access(current_user, resource, method):
  - if resource is None: return respond_404()
  - if resource.owner_id == current_user.id: return allow
  - if current_user.is_superuser:
      - if method in [GET]: return allow
      - if method in [PUT, PATCH, DELETE]: return respond_403_read_only()
  - else: return respond_404()
- Use this helper in each handler so behavior is consistent.

8) Tests / acceptance cases to implement
- Superuser reads own resource -> 200 and full access; can update/delete own resource -> allowed.
- Superuser reads someone else’s resource -> 200 (read-only); superuser attempts to PUT/DELETE someone else’s resource -> 403 with {"detail":"Read-only access"}.
- Normal user reads own resource -> 200; updates/deletes own resource -> allowed.
- Normal user attempts to GET/PUT/DELETE someone else’s resource -> 404.
- Any user requests non-existent resource id -> 404.
- Create (POST) with client-supplied owner_id: stored owner_id equals current_user.id.

9) Implementation checklist
- Ensure authentication middleware populates current_user.id and current_user.is_superuser.
- Ensure resource fetch returns None when not found; do not throw or map to other status.
- Ensure consistent JSON content-type for error responses and exact detail message for the required 403 case.
- Ensure updates and deletes check ownership after fetch and before performing changes.
- Ensure owner_id is never taken from client input on create or update (server-controlled).

Notes and constraints (explicit):
- These instructions apply only to per-resource endpoints (single-resource GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE and POST create). Do not change global list endpoints behavior unless explicitly required.
- Do not reveal existence of other users’ resources to normal users: return 404 for them.
- The only case returning 403 for other-users’ resources is when current_user is a superuser and the method is an update or delete; that 403 must include detail = "Read-only access".

Deliverable: implement the helper, update the handlers for GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE/POST as above, and add unit/integration tests for the acceptance cases listed."}
